9. Integration into clinical workflow
As discussed throughout this manuscript, intraoperative tis-
sue deformations are key limitations to accurate neuronaviga-
tion during neurosurgery. Despite rigid registration of preoper-
ative imaging to the patient positioning in the OR, intraopera-
tive factors render navigation increasingly inaccurate as surgery
progresses. There is a typical TRE of approximately 1–2 mm at
the start of a case that can drift to 4–6 mm, and cortical surface
displacements exceeding 20 mm have been reported in long re-
sections (Stieglitz et al., 2013; Gerard et al., 2021). Intraoper-
ative imaging, such as iUS and iMRI, can partially restore ac-
curacy to the 2–3 mm range, depending on imaging quality and
registration method (Machado et al., 2018, 2019; Gerard et al.,
2021; Dixon et al., 2022). Although these results demonstrate
the potential of intraoperative updates, the need for faster, au-
tomated, and less labor-intensive methods has led to the explo-
ration of AI-based deformation modeling to predict and correct
for brain shift.
Clinically, the performance expectations for AI-driven brain
shift correction mirror those of gold-standard navigation sys-
tems.
Most neuronavigation platforms target a TRE of 2–3
mm for intraoperative guidance (Gerard et al., 2021), and re-
search prototypes aim to meet this threshold while maintain-
ing clinically feasible latency. Although instantaneous updates
would ideally reflect the continuous nature of brain deforma-
tion, this remains computationally unrealistic in practice. A
more pragmatic trade-off between speed and accuracy has de-
veloped that targets update times of 30–60 seconds while main-
taining sub-3 mm accuracy (Haouchine et al., 2023; Rahmani
et al., 2024). Continuous correction may not be essential in
most workflows; instead, updates are integrated at key surgi-
cal checkpoints, such as postdural opening, mid-resection, and
preclosure or pre-iMRI. Using these checkpoints could be suffi-
cient to maintain navigation usability and reduce surgeons’ cog-
nitive load. These periodic updates align well with the natural
pauses in resection and allow computational processes to run
alongside the surgical workflow.
Early demonstrations of AI-assisted deformation modeling
highlight its potential to extend these checkpoint updates be-
yond simple image registration. Promising methods leverage
navigated tool-tip tracking (Juvekar et al., 2023), surgical mi-
croscope video feeds (Haouchine et al., 2023), and ultrasound
sweep acquisitions (Zeineldin et al., 2021; Rahmani et al.,
2024; Aziz et al., 2025), which enable data-driven estimation of
tissue deformation without introducing new hardware. By em-
bedding these models within existing navigation systems, they
can provide updates that complement standard intraoperative
imaging.
The practical performance targets for such systems are
guided by clinical workflow constraints. To preserve surgical
flow, updates should be computed in under one minute, main-
tain 3 mm TRE or less, and present results in a manner that is
immediately interpretable to the surgeon (Safdar et al., 2023).
Visualizations that display deformation as vector fields, color-
coded overlays, or uncertainty maps allow surgeons to under-
stand the reliability of corrections while focusing on the opera-
tive field (Geshvadi et al., 2025)). Moreover, pre-surgical data
synthesis has been explored as a means to preload expected de-
formation maps, which reduce update delays intraoperatively
and allow for timely updates once new imaging or instrument-
tracking data are acquired (Haouchine et al., 2023)). The inte-
gration of these predictive and visualization frameworks reflects
a shift toward surgeon-centered design, where models operate
in the background and present clinically relevant updates only
when accuracy gains are meaningful.
In current clinical practice, brain shift compensation is still
predominantly achieved through conventional rigid or nonrigid
image fusion techniques rather than fully deep learning-based
registration systems. Commercial neuronavigation platforms,
such as those developed by Brainlab SE (Munich, Germany)
and Medtronic plc (Dublin, Ireland), typically rely on semi-
automated rigid or locally constrained alignment between pre-
operative images and intra-operative modalities, such as ultra-
sound or MRI. These approaches aim to update navigation ac-
curacy without performing full deformable re-registration, of-
fering practical improvements in surgical guidance while re-
maining computationally efficient and clinically reliable. Al-
though such systems do not incorporate deep learning, they
represent important translational milestones toward adaptive
neuronavigation. Future clinical solutions are likely to inte-
grate these established workflows with data-driven deformation
models, enabling continuous correction between intra-operative
imaging updates and supporting more seamless multimodal and
deformation-aware navigation.
Looking forward, the barriers to widespread clinical adop-
tion are multifactorial. Among them are computational burden,
data heterogeneity, image quality variability, and the gap be-
19


tween technical validation and clinical evidence (Gerard et al.,
2021; Dixon et al., 2022). Also, models trained on homoge-
neous institutional datasets may fail when exposed to new scan-
ners, protocols, or pathologies (Baheti et al., 2021; Zeineldin
et al., 2021). To advance clinical integration, developers should
prioritize: 1) computational efficiency to enable rapid, clini-
cally relevant updates; 2) interpretable outputs such as defor-
mation overlays and uncertainty estimates that support surgi-
cal decision-making; 3) robust multi-institutional generaliza-
tion through open and diverse training datasets; and 4) prospec-
tive, outcome-linked validation demonstrating measurable im-
provements in extent of resection and postoperative outcomes.
Finally, regulatory and ethical frameworks will need to evolve
alongside these technologies.
FDA clearance for predictive
deformation tools will require transparent safety metrics and
clinician oversight, ensuring that such models act as decision-
support systems that will aid, but never completely replace, a
neurosurgeon’s judgment.
10. Discussion
Image-guided neurosurgery relies on the integration of imag-
ing data acquired at different stages of the surgical process,
including the preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative
phases, to support accurate planning, navigation, decision-
making, and outcome assessment. Each stage presents unique
technical and methodological challenges related to image align-
ment, tissue deformation, and data interpretation. Among these,
discrepancies between preoperative planning images and the
evolving intraoperative or postoperative anatomy remain a ma-
jor source of uncertainty in neuronavigation and surgical eval-
uation. Addressing these discrepancies requires continuous ad-
vances in image registration, modeling, and multimodal data
integration. Recent work in this field has explored a range of
strategies to improve spatial and temporal consistency across
imaging stages. These efforts span biomechanical modeling of
tissue deformation, intraoperative imaging updates using MRI
or ultrasound, the use of microscope-based surface data to re-
fine cortical displacement alignment, and postoperative assess-
ments that evaluate surgical accuracy and tissue change.
In this review, we examined recent computational meth-
ods for brain deformation compensation in IGN, following the
PRISMA 2020 guidelines. From an initial pool of 712 records
identified across multiple databases, 41 studies met the in-
clusion criteria, which specifically targeted methods address-
ing deformations directly induced by neurosurgical interven-
tions. This excluded most works performing inter-patient, atlas-
based, or non-resection registration, as these fail to capture
the complex, topology-altering deformations that occur during
surgery. Research activity in this field has increased steadily
from 2020 to 2025, with a marked rise following the release
of the BraTS-Reg challenge in 2022. Compared with earlier
benchmarks such as the 2017 CuRIOUS challenge, BraTS-Reg
offered a substantially larger volume of data (albeit limited to
MRI) with thorough benchmarking. Together with the rapid
adoption of DL, a surge in learning-based registration research
is clearly observed: DL now dominates the literature, repre-
senting nearly three-quarters of the reviewed studies. However,
this dominance does not necessarily equate to superior perfor-
mance, particularly in multimodal registration, where classic
methods often continue to outperform learning-based ones.
A wide variety of techniques have been proposed to ad-
dress medical image registration in IGN. Researchers have ex-
plored novel similarity functions, strategies to model the ab-
sence of correspondences, and architectures designed to accel-
erate registration through DL. Yet, these challenges remain far
from solved. Handling the large domain gap between multi-
modal images continues to be a major open problem, as cur-
rent similarity metrics often fail to capture both shared and
modality-specific information.
Furthermore, modeling topo-
logical changes such as resections remains difficult, as it con-
flicts with the smoothness and continuity assumptions under-
lying most regularization schemes. In practice, for demand-
ing tasks such as preoperative MRI to iUS registration, state-
of-the-art performance is still achieved with iterative optimiza-
tion methods that are computationally intensive and unsuitable
for real-time use. Finally, there is a critical need to quantify
the registration output in a way that can be interpreted by sur-
geons. Landmark-based approaches, which explicitly identify
correspondences, provide more interpretable results but still un-
derperform dense, deformation-based models in accuracy. Ad-
dressing these limitations, through learned similarity metrics,
topology-aware transformations, and uncertainty-aware infer-
ence, remains crucial to advance toward robust and clinically
deployable registration systems.
Robust biomechanical models of brain deformation, despite
significant advancements, remain largely research tools with
limited clinical adoption. Their main advantage lies in physical
interpretability, explicitly modeling tissue mechanics and BCs
to yield anatomically plausible deformations, even with sparse
intraoperative data. Yet, these models are constrained by high
computational cost, sensitivity to meshing and segmentation
quality, and dependence on uncertain patient-specific material
properties. Validation is further limited by the absence of dense
ground-truth deformation data, often reduced to sparse land-
mark or image-based comparisons. Recent DL approaches, no-
tably PINNs and graph- or point-based networks, have begun to
mitigate these issues by embedding physical laws into the learn-
ing process. These models eliminate explicit meshing, achieve
real-time performance, and generalize across geometries and
BCs while maintaining biomechanical plausibility. However,
robust estimation of tissue material properties remains a ma-
jor bottleneck, as these parameters vary widely across patients
and are rarely measurable in vivo. Progress toward integrating
multimodal intraoperative data to dynamically infer such prop-
erties will be key to achieving real-time, patient-specific, and
physics-consistent modeling for IGN.
Validation practices across the field are evolving alongside
these modeling advances. Traditional geometric metrics such as
TRE and Dice score continue to serve as the backbone for quan-
titative assessment, but they inadequately represent the confi-
dence or stability of predictions. Recent efforts are shifting to-
ward uncertainty-aware validation, where calibration metrics,
20


probabilistic scores, and correlation analyses between predicted
confidence and empirical error are used to evaluate trustworthi-
ness. Large-scale datasets such as BraTS-Reg, RESECT, and
ReMIND provide the necessary diversity for cross-institutional
benchmarking, but the field still lacks standardized protocols
and challenge environments specifically tailored to uncertainty
estimation. Establishing these shared validation frameworks,
together with consistent reporting of statistical significance and
cross-domain testing, will be important for regulatory accep-
tance and reproducibility.
Future progress will depend on connecting uncertainty mod-
eling with actionable clinical insight and aligning it with the
broader demands of real-world deployment. Beyond predic-
tive accuracy, registration systems must satisfy constraints of
speed, robustness, interpretability, and seamless integration into
surgical workflows.
Intraoperative use demands near real-
time inference with minimal preprocessing, intuitive visual-
ization of results, and resilience to variations in imaging pro-
tocols, anatomy, and pathology. Rather than treating uncer-
tainty as a static visualization artifact, it should guide adap-
tive decision-making: triggering data reacquisition, confidence-
weighted fusion, or surgeon alerts when reliability falls below
critical thresholds. Hybrid strategies that combine predictive
and probabilistic elements, alongside semi-supervised or con-
tinual learning frameworks that leverage both real and syn-
thetic data, may offer the most practical route toward this goal.
Ultimately, the success of models that account for brain shift
will be defined not solely by geometric accuracy but by their
ability to operate as trustworthy, interpretable, and workflow-
compatible systems that enhance surgical confidence and pa-
tient safety when accuracy is most critical.

Abstract: Accurate compensation of brain deformation is a critical challenge for reliable image-guided neurosurgery, as surgical manipulation and tumor resection induce tissue motion that misaligns preoperative planning images with intraoperative anatomy and longitudinal studies. In this systematic review, we synthesize recent AI-driven approaches developed between January 2020 and April 2025 for modeling and correcting brain deformation. A comprehensive literature search was conducted in PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Web of Science, with predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria focused on computational methods applied to brain defor- mation compensation for neurosurgical imaging, resulting in 41 studies meeting these criteria. We provide a unified analysis of methodological strategies, including deep learning-based image registration, direct deformation field regression, synthesis-driven multimodal alignment, resection-aware architectures addressing missing correspondences, and hybrid models that integrate biome- chanical priors. We also examine dataset utilization, reported evaluation metrics, validation protocols, and how uncertainty and generalization have been assessed across studies. While AI-based deformation models demonstrate promising performance and computational efficiency, current approaches exhibit limitations in out-of-distribution robustness, standardized benchmarking, in- terpretability, and readiness for clinical deployment. Our review highlights these gaps and outlines opportunities for future research aimed at achieving more robust, generalizable, and clinically translatable deformation compensation solutions for neurosurgical guidance. By organizing recent advances and critically evaluating evaluation practices, this work provides a comprehensive foun- dation for researchers and clinicians engaged in developing and applying AI-based brain deformation methods.
